Widawa Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Widawa, Poland

Not demolished. Widawa, founded in 1388 and downgraded from city status in 1870, saw Jewish settlement documented from the 18th century; population reached 48% (632) by 1827, with an autonomous kehilla formed in 1838. Germans killed the community's last rabbi, Mordechaj Maroko, by burning him alive along with his Torah scroll; a 1940 ghetto held roughly 100 families, with 728 residents transported to Bełchatów in December 1941 and the remainder sent to Chełmno by summer 1942. This cemetery, probably founded in the 18th century, received its last recorded burial in 1940 before German destruction; only one tombstone remains at the original site. In 2021, funded by Widawa's County Hall and organized by Jacek Frąckiewicz, over 100 tombstones dated 1924-1938 were recovered from a pavement beside a mill on the Naciecz River in Wola Kleszczowa and returned, now serving as the basis for a hundred memorial plaques honoring those buried here.
